AJK.name: Juneau
AJK.excerpt: Confidence is high on cold air moving in at the surface Monday, along with moisture timing Tuesday and Wednesday. Largest uncertainty is how warm will the incoming airmass be and how quickly we can scrub out any persistent cold air at the surface.

sections.name: Synopsis
paragraphs: - Continued periods of light rain for Icy Strait Corridor and southward Friday along with some patchy fog and drizzle.
- Another system moves in for Friday night into Saturday, bringing slightly increased winds and more rain from Yakutat to around Sumner Strait.
- Drier and cooler weather for Sunday with fog chances for Saturday into Sunday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The current front moving over the panhandle is bringing more low clouds and cooler conditions in its wake. A couple noteworthy points for this front for the northern inner channels. Temperatures continue to be cooler than expected, and with weak forcing, periods of freezing drizzle are occurring in the Haines area. Not expecting ice accumulation, as additional moisture and ice in the clouds look to transition this to more of a rain snow mix, leaning a bit stronger into snow until easterly winds can kick in past 6 PM tonight. May also see some brief snow with minor accumulations up on the Klondike Highway and parts of Skagway, though moisture is struggling to get into the valley.

Saturday sees the "stronger" front move into the area. The major change with this system is the inclusion of up to 2 inches for the Klondike Highway. Most of the moisture appears to be low level, below 700 mb, though orographic lift from south to southwesterlies are expected to bring snowy conditions. Above the 700 mb layer, stronger southwesterlies across the Chilkat Range do look to shadow, with Haines not expecting much precipitation at all, and somewhat more stable flow limiting lift over the Klondike, hence the lower snow totals. Expect most of this to be wrapped up within 12 hours of snow onset, as this front moves through the area quickly. Beyond this front, ridging and surface high pressure builds, bringing widespread fog chances overnight Saturday into Sunday. Confidence for fog development is high, but confidence is medium for fog duration. Like last time, this fog has the very real possibility to stick around all day, particularly in sheltered locations like the back of Mendenhall Valley.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: /Sunday through Wednesday/... Sunday continues to look like one fine day across Southeast, with the potential for some fog development. Stay tuned. Mariners moving around the inner channels should be aware of outflow winds, especially overnight into Monday as high pressure builds across the Yukon and BC provinces. One impact from outflow will be cold air once again infiltrating the Panhandle, especially those closest to the Coast Range and major river inlets, priming us for snow. Expect a large system to move in off the Bering Monday steering plenty of moisture into our area Tuesday into Wednesday. Snow impacts will be directly tied to how prolific the outflow event is for the start of next week, the resulting cold air infiltration, and how quickly relatively warmer southerlies can scrub out the cold airmass at the surface. For now, the published forecast reflects minor snow for some communities separate from Haines and Skagway. It certainly feels like the first snow event for us humble few in Southeast; however, accumulating snow (outside of the Haines and Klondike highways) looks modest, likely only some flakes to perhaps an inch before turning to rain. Yakutat will also see some snow Tuesday. Stay tuned as we monitor for developments thru the weekend.

Confidence is high on cold air moving in at the surface Monday, along with moisture timing Tuesday and Wednesday. Largest uncertainty is how warm will the incoming airmass be and how quickly we can scrub out any persistent cold air at the surface. While it looks like a decent overrunning setup, the limiting factor is the duration of the Monday outflow, limiting snow potential.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Come Tuesday, the low that sent the previous shortwave through open and phase with a deeper low approaching the SoCal coast. Flow becoming increasingly southwesterly will steer a plume of moisture northward.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Valley rain and mountain snow through early Saturday. Snow levels 7000-9000 feet dropping to 5500-7500 feet as precipitation ends.
- Gusty winds in southern areas with cold frontal passage tonight.
- Unsettled pattern continues with near or above normal temperatures through next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Rain and high mountain snow will continue as westerly flow funnels deep moisture into the region ahead of an approaching upper level trough. The air mass remains relatively mild ahead of the upper wave which will keep snow levels elevated. The rain/snow line will range from around 7kft across the e-central Oregon and w-central Idaho mountains to around 9kft along the northern NV border. This will limit the heavier accumulating snow to higher mtns for much of tonight. Precipitation will spread south and east through the evening as the upper wave and accompanying cold front track inland. Forcing along the front will enhance precipitation rates, especially across higher terrain and would expect to see a period of moderate rain/snow in advance of the front. Mountains across the region will see another 0.25-0.50" of liquid with the focus of heaviest precipitation over the Boise mtns. Here additional liquid totals of 0.5-1.0" are expected. Snow levels will drop with the frontal passage which could bring minor accumulations to valley floors in w-central Idaho mtn valleys including McCall, Yellowpine, and Warm Lake.

The cold frontal passage will bring gusty winds to open and elevated terrain overnight. Strongest winds are forecast across SE Oregon, and the Snake Plain and highlands of SW Idaho. Most sites will see gusts between 25-40 mph with windier locations near Steens Mtn, Owyhee Mtns and s-central Idaho seeing gusts to 50 mph. The strongest winds will be shortlived, 1 to 2 hours, with breezy conditions continuing for several more hours behind the front. Most sites will see winds diminish by mid- morning.

Saturday is dry across the region, minus a few showers lingering in the southern mtns. Sheltered valleys will see patchy fog develop, though increasing clouds and easterly winds will likely inhibit widespread development. Sunday starts dry with showers moving into SE Oregon on Sunday, then spreading into SW Idaho Sunday night as the next storm system approaches the coast. Snow levels will range 6-7.5kft as light to moderate precipitation starts.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A shortwave trough passing across the area on Monday will bring the next shot of widespread precipitation across the area. The southerly flow precursing this trough will result in initial snow levels of 6.5-8.5kft MSL, dropping down to 5.5-7kft MSL Monday afternoon. These snow levels will limit any significant snow accumulations to higher terrain in the West Central Idaho Mountains. Some high elevation passes will likely experience winter driving conditions Monday morning into Monday afternoon, with 6 to 8 inches of snow forecast for Highway 21 near and on Banner Summit. Monday will also feature gusty conditions, with gusts to 25-35 kt south and west of the Snake River Plain and along SW-Idaho ridge tops.

Come Tuesday, the low that sent the previous shortwave through open and phase with a deeper low approaching the SoCal coast. Flow becoming increasingly southwesterly will steer a plume of moisture northward. As of now it looks like the bulk of this moisture will remain south and east of our CWA, although it will allow for a 30- 40% chance of precipitation for the western Magic Valley and Owyhee/Camas Counties. While some uncertainty remains in the exact track of the SoCal low, ensembles favor it progressing through the Desert Southwest. This track will keep our area out of the deformation zone and dry mid-week as a positively tilted trough builds over our area. Uncertainty increases late week-next week, although most guidance resolves a weak shortwave crossing over Thursday into Friday. Moisture availability is in question with this shortwave, with low precipitation chances, although at the very least it will bring increased cloud cover. Temperatures through the long-term period will remain near or slightly above normal.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: The latest runs were still trending toward at least a weak closed low tracking a bit further northward into Colorado toward Thursday. This will mean another chance of rain/snow for the forecast area with temperatures cooling to near normal levels again.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Hazardous travel tonight - Saturday evening for the northern mountains and I-70 mountain corridor due to snow and blowing snow. Snowfall amounts greater than 12" likely in the northern tier of mountains.
- Snow squalls possible with greatest threat in the mountains late morning to early afternoon Saturday.

- Banded snow (initially mixed with rain) for the the plains and I-25 Corridor Saturday to early Saturday evening. Brief heavy snow but generally light accumulations possible. Potential (50-60% chance) for Denver's first measurable snowfall of the season.
- Gusty winds along the Front Range and northern border area into this evening, spreading across all the plains Saturday.
- Return of mostly dry weather Sunday - Tuesday, next disturbance may arrive by Wednesday or Thursday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Gusty winds but mild temperatures are present along the Front Range this afternoon. The winds will slowly decrease in the lower elevations with the loss of daytime heating and mixing, but remain quite gusty over the higher foothills and mountains where gusts of 40-60 mph will continue through the night under the influence of strong westerly flow aloft. We are starting to see the first signs of our next snow event, with mid level clouds thickening in the northern mountains and even a few flurries noted on the Rocky Mountain National Park cam. While moisture is rather limited below about 700 mb, we do expect a further but moderated increase in snow overnight. That will occur as we get into the left exit region of the upper level jet and a fast moving shortwave (still out in the Pacific) starts to bring large scale lift to the forecast area.

That shortwave and associated cold front will sweep across the area Saturday late morning to early afternoon. A period of pre- frontal gusty downslope winds to 40-60 mph can be expected across the Front Range Foothills and adjacent plains, but then expect a sharp turn to strong, gusty north winds behind the cold front. There is still uncertainty with the timing of this front. Yesterday, models were aggressive in speeding this front up with a morning passage. However, today they've been delaying the frontal arrival til around noon or shortly thereafter. We still think it might be late morning as the trough position and precipitation loading/sub-cloud evaporation in Wyoming would support an earlier arrival. Whatever the case, strong, gusty winds to 40-55 mph can be expected on the plains with and just behind the frontal passage. Slight anticyclonic turning is also noted, which will negate the downslope component and combine with synoptic scale lift of the trough passage and a brief period of strong frontogenesis to allow showers to spread southward across the plains. Initially, temperatures may support a little rain, but the magnitude of cold advection and surface temperatures dropping into the 30s would support mostly snow within an hour or so of the frontal passage.

The strong frontogenesis, slight instability (even a bit of SBCAPE noted along the front), moisture convergence, and neutral to slightly unstable mid level lapse rates will also bring a threat of snow squalls. The highest probability (60%) for those would be in the mountains during and just behind the frontal passage, and possibly (20-40% chance) down into the foothills and Palmer Divide where temperatures would be colder and more conducive to road impacts. The greatest risk time would be with the front, starting around 10 am (northern mountains), pushing south through early afternoon and ending in the southern portions of the forecast area closer to 2 pm.

Regarding snowfall amounts, many favorable ingredients are coming together for moderate to heavy snow totals in the high country. These include synoptic scale lift, strong orographics turning more northwesterly and eventually favoring Summit County later in the event, and neutral to slightly unstable lapse rates. While there is still some uncertainty, we have modest confidence of 5-12 inch totals for the Front Range mountains and Summit County (heaviest north of I-70) and 8-16 inch amounts for the northern Gore and Park Ranges. If anything, those could be on the light side if we happen to have more moisture and overproduce tonight. We are somewhat leery of the heaviest totals offered up by some of the high resolution models, but something to keep an eye on as we start this event tonight. On the plains, any accumulation will be heavily dependent on the intensity and persistence of snow showers/bands. At this point, it still looks like areas north of metro Denver will only see a brief dusting or no accumulation, but a growing chance of light accumulations as one heads southward through Denver metro and especially into the Palmer Divide and southern Front Range foothills due to the deep northerly or even slight NNE flow. That would help longevity there. Thus, we've bumped up totals a little into the foothills west and southwest of Denver with 1-3 inches most likely there. We're still carrying a 50-60% chance of Denver's first official measurable snow (DIA), but it would likely be light (less than 0.5") if we do see any accumulation.

We still expect snow to taper off fairly quickly from north to south late Saturday afternoon and early Saturday evening as the system quickly ejects to the east. However, some travel impacts may linger in the mountains and southern foothills into early Sunday morning due to residual road snow. Those conditions will improve rather quickly however with return of sunshine, so Sunday is shaping up to be a much better post-holiday travel day than Saturday.

Mainly dry weather will then persist into Monday and Tuesday, although the flow appears to become zonal enough to have a chance of light snow showers for the high country. After a chilly Sunday, temperatures will be warming back to above normal levels both days.

The latest runs were still trending toward at least a weak closed low tracking a bit further northward into Colorado toward Thursday. This will mean another chance of rain/snow for the forecast area with temperatures cooling to near normal levels again.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Heading into the long term period, starting on Sunday, ridging noses in for the morning hours behind the system that impacted the forecast area on Saturday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Heavy mountain snow will increase in coverage Friday evening through the overnight hours, with peak gusts as high as 65 mph.
- A strong cold front will sweep through the area late Saturday morning, bringing colder temperatures and snow.
- Saturday's snowfall may be locally heavy, with reduced visibility in falling and blowing snow and minor accumulations impacting holiday travel.
- Another round of strong winds is possible (50% chance) in the wind prone areas Sunday through early Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: We head into the weekend with a more active pattern in place, with a progressive storm system bringing our area heavy mountain snow, high wind conditions, and some light snowfall accumulations to much of the lower elevations across SE Wyoming and the Nebraska Panhandle. Another mild albeit breezy day is in store for us today, with many locations along the I-80 corridor seeing gusts up to 65 mph as a vigorous 55-65 knot 700 mb speed maximum noses into our area from the WNW. Under the downslope flow regime and windy conditions, high temperatures this afternoon are expected to soar well into the low to mid 50s east of the Laramie Range, with cooler 40s to the west where cloud cover is thicker and more abundant ahead of our next system that will begin to impact the region this evening into Saturday afternoon. Some higher gusts of 45-50 mph have been observed this morning in/around Cheyenne, but have since held well- below high wind criteria, so have not upgraded the High Wind Watch to a warning for Zone 118 at this time (Cheyenne and I-25 across Northern Laramie County. Wind gusts along the I-80 corridor at the wind-prone sites have exceeding 60-65 mph this morning into the early afternoon, so will continue the High Wind Warning for these zones until tomorrow evening when winds are expected to die off rather quickly based off in-house random forest guidance.

The main updates to the forecast involve upgrading the Winter Weather Advisory to a Winter Storm Warning for the Sierra Madre Range, as QPF has increased have snow levels have decreased since the previous forecast package. Although this clipper-type system will be progressive, models have trended higher with liquid totals over the last 24 hours, therefore increasing confidence of exceeding warning criteria for the Sierra Madre Range, which yesterday seemed to be a borderline event with upper-end advisory criteria. Blustery conditions combined with periods of moderate to heavy snow above 8000 feet will also create areas of blowing snow and reduced visibilities down to 1/4 of a mile or less, so please take extra precautions if traveling through these areas.

For the lower elevations, a cold front will rapidly slice across the area sometime mid morning into the early afternoon hours, which has trended more progressive over the past few global model cycles. As the cold front is expected to be rather sharp, temperatures are expected to plunge into the low 30s to upper 20s by sunset, with our high temperatures likely being observed in the late morning hours pre-frontal passage. Though wind speeds will decrease to well-below high wind criteria, can still expect blustery conditions behind the front with wind chill values down into the teens and low 20s, so it will be a good afternoon and evening to warm up with some hot leftover turkey or warm gravy.

Now for the "S" word we have all been wondering about...Will it snow on the lower elevations? Most signs point to yes which is the good news. This will likely go down as our first measurable snowfall of the season for Cheyenne (and latest on record), but not expecting snowfall totals to amount to anything more than an inch or two east of the I-25 corridor, with the exception of areas along and north of the Pine Ridge and locations on the northern periphery of the Laramie Range (i.e. Douglas and Glenrock). Prior to the frontal passage, expecting mainly westerly or northwesterly winds in locations such as Cheyenne and Wheatland, which promotes downsloping off the higher terrain to the west, and therefore drying and warming. This isn't ideal for snow (or moisture for that matter) for these locations, so it is mainly post-frontal passage when the winds turn more out of the north where we can expect to see our greatest chances for snow. As temperatures are anticipated to rapidly drop behind the front, am not expecting an elongated transition period from rain to snow.

As mentioned earlier, locations where the northerly/northwesterly anafrontal flow is more upslope such as along and north of the windward slopes of the Northern Laramie Range and the Northern portion of the Pine Ridge, some totals may manage to crack 2 inches by the time all this is done, but didn't have enough confidence to increase totals to advisory criteria across lower elevations of Converse and Niobrara Counties at this time due to the quick progression of the system. Any lingering snow showers should begin to exit the region early tomorrow evening, with clouds decreasing in coverage and winds beginning to wind down. With any fresh snow cover on the ground, plus clearing skies and calmer conditions in the post-frontal air mass, can expect a much chillier night overnight Saturday relative to what we have seen these past couple of days, with many locations falling well into the teens by early Sunday morning.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Heading into the long term period, starting on Sunday, ridging noses in for the morning hours behind the system that impacted the forecast area on Saturday. As we progress into the day on Sunday, by the afternoon hours, the ridge flattens with the upper level flow becoming zonal. This pattern will keep us dry, but a by product will be the increased possibility for strong winds in our known wind prones along I-25 and I-80. The 700 mb flow ramps up late Sunday with speeds approaching 50 knots and remains so through the overnight hours with the flow increasing further through Monday as speeds approach 60 knots by the late afternoon into the evening hours. With ample subsidence, negative Omega (GFS), these stronger winds have a good chance of making it down to the surface. As such, our in-house guidance indicates up to a 65% chance of high winds at Arlington/Elk Mountain, around a 40% chance along the I-80 Summit, and near 55% chance at Bordeaux for later in the day on Sunday into Monday. As we head into Tuesday, conditons look to be relatively quiet outside of a two weak shortwaves that will slide through, the first on Tuesday and another one on Wednesday. These won't bring widespread chances of precipitation but increase the threat across the mountains for the two aforementioned days. Beyond Wednesday, a transient ridge noses back in and controls weather heading into next weekend. Switching gears a bit and taking a look at temperatures, Sunday will start off chilly with lows in the upper teens to low 20s and don't expect temperatures to warm much as a cold airmass will be in place as highs only climb into the upper 30s to low 40s west of the I-25 corridor and low 40s off to the east. These cooler temperatures are short-lived, as warm air advects into the region, highs will climb back into the 40s west of I-25 and low to mid 50s east of the I-25 corridor by Monday. These "warmer" temperatures will persist through Wednesday, then look for cooler temperatures to return at the tail end of next week.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: A transitory ridge will slide in for Sunday and Monday with drier conditions expected.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Snow will begin along the northern Divide this evening, lingering through Sunday morning. Snow totals of 10-15 inches are expected for the Park and Elkhead mountains, with 4-8 inches across the Flat Tops and Central Divide Mountains.
- Winds gusting 40 to 50 mph are expected with this system this evening through Saturday night, leading to blowing and drifting snow and difficult driving conditions over the mountain passes.
- An unsettled pattern looks to continue into next week with potential for more mountain snow by mid week, but details remain uncertain.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Mid and high clouds continue to spill in from the northwest as a strong atmospheric river carried by a low pressure trough pushes into the Pacific Northwest as seen on satellite imagery. This moisture is being carried up and over a high pressure ridge sitting over the Desert Southwest but is showing signs of breaking down. Conditions this afternoon will remain dry with showers increasing this evening over the northern mountains as this moisture moves into the northern portion of our CWA. Anticipate mild temperatures about 5 degrees above normal this afternoon.
MOUNTAIN SNOWFALL TONIGHT THROUGH SATURDAY NIGHT:

A strong 140 kt jet will accompany this rather robust shortwave as it tracks through the Intermountain West and Northern Rockies with the jet setting up tonight over northern Utah into southwest Colorado, with the northern and central Colorado mountains in the more favored area for strong lift. Specific humidity climbs above 4 g/kg with PWAT anomalies above 200 percent of normal across the north so even though we are on the tail end of this AR moisture as it moves further inland, we will have plenty to work with. The strongest period of forcing looks to occur Saturday morning into the early afternoon, with the highest snowfall rates expected between 5 am and 5 pm Saturday. This is a favorable setup for strong northwest orographics in addition to the dynamics and QG forcing during this time. Post- Thanksgiving travel will be impacted during the morning and evening commutes on Saturday so be prepared for difficult winter driving conditions with blowing snow also contributing to reduced visibilities as winds are expected to gust 40 to 50 mph over the higher terrain and passes. The lower elevations could see winds gusting 30 to 40 mph as well at times but look to remain rain if anything. The impacts will be in the northern and central mountains with the Park Range on track to receive 10 to 15 inches. Probabilities of over a foot of snow is highest in the Park Range with chances 70 to 80 percent, so the Winter Storm Warning remains on track with Winter Weather Advisories for the Flattops and Gore and Elk Mountains including the I-70 mountain corridor through Vail and Vail Pass where 4 to 8 inches of snow is expected. Timing of these winter highlights is 5 pm today through 5 am Sunday as snow looks to continue through early Sunday morning.

A transitory ridge will slide in for Sunday and Monday with drier conditions expected. Some high clouds will continue to pass overhead due to another system moving into the Pacific Northwest but this one doesn't appear to impact us much as it tracks to our northwest as it moves inland and weakens. The next potential weather maker to watch for is another AR and low pressure trough that moves onto the west coast Tuesday and potentially brings more mountain snowfall to our region during the mid week timeframe. There is still quite a bit of model uncertainty with this system with differences in timing and storm track. The GFS takes a more southerly track with this low becoming closed off and splitting as it tracks south of the Four Corners through Arizona and New Mexico Wednesday evening through Thursday. The ECMWF track is a bit further north coming in as an open wave trough but still favoring the southern mountains. Model guidance remains in relatively poor agreement, with significant spread. The southerly track does increase potential for atmospheric river moisture to accompany this system. However, the exact track of this system can make the difference between a solid mountain snowfall and seeing little to no snow at all. We shall have to wait and see how the forecast for this system develops over the coming days.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Northwest flow moderates through the day Sunday, with more westerly flow in the forecast trough early next week, leading to warmer and drier conditions areawide.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Snow increases in coverage across the Central Mountains late tonight, with snow and blowing snow producing hazardous travel conditions through the day Saturday into Saturday night.
- A strong cold front to move across the Plains Saturday with Medium Confidence (40-50 percent) of winds 55 to 65 mph behind the passing system.
- Higher confidence (60-70 percent) for snow and blowing snow across the Pikes Peak/Palmer Dvd region Saturday afternoon/evening.
- Warming and drying trend through early next week, with more unsettled weather in the offing for the middle to end of the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Current water vapor imagery and upper air analysis moderate west to northwest flow across the region, with short wave energy moving onshore across the Pacific Northwest Coast at this time. Water vapor imagery has ample moisture embedded within the flow leading to periods of wave clouds spilling across the plains at this time.

Latest models in good agreement of increasing northwest flow across the region tonight with strong northwest flow in place through the day tomorrow, as the Pacific Northwest embedded wave digs across the Intermountain West and into the Rockies. This will bring increasing coverage of orographic snowfall to the Central Mtns overnight, especially across the higher terrain north of Cottonwood Pass. Breezy northwest winds of 30 to 60 mph will continue will also continue over the high terrain as well, with DESI indicating a very low potential (10-20 percent) of said stronger winds of 60 mph spilling across the immediate adjacent plains into the I-25 Corridor through early Saturday morning.

Snow will increase in coverage and intensity through the day across the Central Mtns before tapering off Saturday evening into early Sunday morning, with accumulations of 3 to 8 inches possible, highest amounts expected north of Cottonwood Pass. In addition, strong northwest winds will lead to hazardous travel in snow and blowing snow, with a Winter Weather Advisory in effect from midnight tonight through midnight Saturday night. The slightly further west location of said passing system will also send a strong cold front across the eastern Plains late Saturday morning and afternoon, with strong gradient flow supporting gusty northerly winds of 55 to 65 mph possible in its wake. Latest DESI has 35-50 percent chance of wind gusts of 60 mph or greater behind this passing front, greatest across the far southeast plains, and with that said, we will keep current high wind watch in place from late Saturday morning through the early evening.

The further west location of the passing trough will also bring a better potential for a quick burst of snow across the plains behind the passing front, especially for northern portions of the Pikes Peak region and along the Palmer Dvd, where a quick 1 to 2 inches of wind driven snow will be possible Saturday afternoon into the early evening. Those planning travel across the Palmer Dvd should stay weather aware Saturday afternoon, as temperatures will rapidly cool leading possible icy/snowpacked roads.
The strongest winds to diminish through early Saturday evening, with the potential for a few snow showers/flurries across the Southern I-25 Corridor and southeast plains into Saturday night.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Northwest flow moderates through the day Sunday, with more westerly flow in the forecast trough early next week, leading to warmer and drier conditions areawide. Latest longer range model and ensemble data supports a split flow pattern developing early next week, with an eastern Pacific system within the southern stream expected to move onshore across the southern California Coast on Tuesday. Model solutions differ on where this system moves from there, with the GFS remaining the furtherest south with the system as it moves across the southern Rockies, where as the Canadian and EC solutions have it further north, bringing the potential for a more significant winter weather system for south central and southeast Colorado in the later Wednesday and Thursday timeframe. Time will tell, if we see the first snowfall across southeast Colorado later next week.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: High pressure will make its way back over the area for Sunday, bringing a day of dry conditions and temperatures on the mild side.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry and mild conditions will persist for much of today, with highs around 5-10F above seasonal normals.
- A weak storm system will move across northern Utah and southwest Wyoming late tonight into Saturday, bringing generally light valley rain and mountain snow.

- Dry conditions will return temporarily on Sunday before another weak system grazes northern Utah on Monday. A more potent system may impact primarily southern Utah for the latter half of the upcoming week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The center of a Pacific ridge has shifted southward toward northern Mexico this morning, bringing a westerly flow aloft to Utah and southwest Wyoming today. The flow will continue to increase today as a Pacific Northwest system moves over the top of this feature. With improved mixing, temperatures will be a bit warmer than yesterday, with maxes averaging 5-10F above seasonal normals.

The weakening trough is expected to track across northern Utah and southwest Wyoming tonight into Saturday morning. Precipitation (valley rain, snow above 6-7kft) will initially be focused near the Utah/Idaho border, shifting south overnight into early Saturday. Accumulations will be light, no more than a few inches for the mountains, but this may cause some brief travel difficulties overnight. Most precipitation will be done Saturday morning, with a few showers expected to linger over the northern mountains into the afternoon hours.

High pressure will make its way back over the area for Sunday, bringing a day of dry conditions and temperatures on the mild side. This is expected to quickly shift east, however, as a rather weak trough grazes northern Utah for Monday, most likely bringing just a few showers near the Utah/Idaho border. Guidance continues to indicate the potential for a broad closed low to move across the Desert Southwest for the latter half of the upcoming week, bringing the potential for cooler temperatures and some more substantial precipitation, at least for southern Utah.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: You can trigger dangerous avalanches near and above treeline on wind-loaded slopes steeper than about 35 degrees. The most dangerous slopes face the north half of the compass. Winds will be strong enough this weekend to move snow above treeline. Give slopes a wide berth where you find recently drifted snow. You can trigger these drifts from adjacent terrain or low-angled slopes.
Seek out wind-sheltered areas and slopes below treeline for safer travel options.

2754.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Dylan Craaybeek
bottom_line: The avalanche danger will worsen throughout the day on Saturday with new snow and strong westerly winds. The most dangerous slopes, where you can trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you, are northeast- and east-facing slopes where the wind-drifted snow is rapidly accumulating on buried weak layers. For safer travel options, seek out wind-sheltered terrain where your feet, skis, or machine easily sink deep into the snow, and you don't see any cracking in the snow as you travel across it.

2690.travel_advice: Very dangerous avalanche conditions. Travel in avalanche terrain not recommended.

product.author: Krista Beyer
bottom_line: A potent storm marks a return of winter and avalanche problems to the Northern Mountains. Heavy precipitation and blowing snow increase avalanche danger throughout the day Saturday. You can trigger a large avalanche in the new snow. The most dangerous slopes are where winds blow snow into thick drifts above weak old snow on north to northeast through east slopes.

Travel in or under avalanche terrain is not recommended in the above treeline elevation band. You can find safer travel options in wind-sheltered terrain, at lower elevations, and on slopes less than about 30 degrees steep.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

1736.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Elevations above 7,000 feet have 1-2 feet of snow on the ground. You may encounter pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north- and east-facing terrain. If the snow feels stiff or slabby underfoot, then find a different aspect away from wind-drifted snow. The biggest hazard remains thin snow cover and hitting rocks, logs, and stumps. Even a small slide through thin coverage could end a season before it even starts.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: Above 7,000 feet, a layered snowpack is beginning to build for the season. Good, albeit thin, skiing and riding conditions have been reported at upper elevations. Elevations below 7,000 feet remain thin and bony. Before November 13th, most slopes were bare. Winter trailhead access remains a challenge as there is not quite enough snow to launch sleds. Most forest roads become impassable by vehicle above 6,500 feet. As folks start poking around the mountains, remember that avalanches can occur with just a few feet of snow on the ground. There may be some lingering pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north and east-facing terrain features, particularly just below ridgelines.

Beginning Thanksgiving Day, a large storm system will impact the Pacific and Interior Northwest. Strong winds, mountain snow, and fluctuating rain/snow levels will be in the cards for several days. Pay attention to changing weather and snow conditions heading into the weekend. Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

Fresh wind slabs will come back onto the menu with more snow and wind later this week. Pay attention to gullies that can become crossloaded and may also act as a terrain trap. Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices. Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
Turn On Your Snow and Avalanche Brain

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).

• Help us paint a picture of what's going on in the mountains. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps forecasters and the public alike.

2755.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Krista Beyer
bottom_line: Avalanche danger will increase throughout the day Saturday as strong winds drift new snow at upper elevations. You can trigger an avalanche where winds drift new snow into thicker and more connected slabs on lee slopes. The most dangerous slopes face north, northeast, and east, where new snow drifts onto a connected layer of weak old grains.
Choose wind-sheltered terrain for safer travel options.

2701.travel_advice: Dangerous avalanche conditions. Careful snowpack evaluation, cautious route-finding and conservative decision-making essential.

product.author: Krista Beyer
bottom_line: A potent storm marks a return of winter and avalanche problems to the Northern Mountains. New snow and strong winds increase avalanche danger throughout the day Saturday. You can trigger a large avalanche in the new snow. The most dangerous slopes are where winds blow snow into thick drifts above weak old snow on north to northeast through east slopes.
You can find safer travel options in wind-sheltered terrain and on slopes less than about 30 degrees steep.
